vignette:
He is eighteen now, a young man from Oceania who speaks with the careful, measured tone of someone used to scanning a room before he says too much. On paper, he is a project manager, unusually young for the role, and people often describe him as mature, dependable, and calm under pressure. By the time he talks about his childhood, it becomes clearer that this steadiness was learned early, and at a cost.

He grows up in a house where evenings are unpredictable. He remembers the sound before he remembers the details: a chair scraping hard across the floor, a cupboard slamming, his mother’s voice changing pitch. As a boy, he lies in bed listening for the pattern of footsteps that tells him whether he should stay still or get up and stand near his younger siblings’ room. He never knows exactly when an argument will become something else, only that it often does. He sees his father shove his mother against a wall in the kitchen, sees a plate break near her feet, sees her flinch before a hand is even raised. He remembers once standing in the hallway, frozen, holding a schoolbook to his chest while his father shouted so loudly that the veins stood out in his neck. His mother catches his eye for a second and gives him a look that says, without words, go back to your room. He obeys, but he does not leave mentally. He listens to every sound until the house goes quiet.

After that, he becomes the child who watches everything. At school he is praised for being responsible. At home he learns how to read danger in tiny changes—a door closed too sharply, a silence that lasts too long, the smell of alcohol, his mother washing dishes with movements that are too quick. He starts sleeping lightly. If he hears raised voices anywhere, even from neighbors, his body tenses before he has time to think. He tells himself he should have done more back then, though he was only a child. That thought stays with him and hardens into something close to shame.

As he gets older, he throws himself into tasks and structure. Planning feels safer than feeling. He likes timelines, checklists, backup options. His work suits this part of him. As a project manager, he keeps track of details others miss, anticipates problems before they happen, and makes sure everyone knows the plan. Colleagues admire his composure. They do not see how rattled he becomes when a meeting turns heated, or how his chest tightens when two coworkers start talking over each other. In those moments, he stops hearing the content and hears only escalation. He stays outwardly composed, but his mind narrows, his shoulders lock, and afterward he needs several minutes alone in a bathroom stall or outside by the loading area to get his breathing under control.

He rarely talks about his childhood directly. Even with his girlfriend, who he cares for deeply, he gives the edited version: “Things were rough at home.” She notices that he startles when someone drops something in the kitchen, that he goes quiet when couples argue in public, that he insists on knowing where the exits are when they go somewhere new. At night he sometimes wakes suddenly, heart pounding, unsure for a moment what year it is. The dreams are not always exact replays, but they carry the same feeling—being trapped in a house full of danger, listening for impact. On those nights, he checks his phone, checks the locks, and tells himself he is not there anymore. Sleep does not come back easily.

He avoids going into detail because once he starts remembering, the images arrive vividly. A broken mug on the floor. His mother’s face turned away. The helplessness of being small and listening. He hates feeling pulled backward like that, so he keeps busy. If he is working, organizing, answering messages, helping someone else solve a problem, he can hold the memories at a distance. But the effort leaves him tired. He describes feeling “on” all the time, as if some part of him is permanently assigned to lookout duty.

What troubles him most in the present is how quickly his body reacts even when his mind knows he is safe. If his girlfriend sounds irritated, he feels a surge of alarm and starts trying to fix things immediately, apologizing before he understands what he has done wrong. If she asks for space during a disagreement, he feels a panicky urgency that reminds him of being shut out of the kitchen doorway as a boy, knowing something bad was happening on the other side. He knows these reactions are bigger than the moment, and that realization frustrates him. He wants closeness, but he is always braced for rupture.

He speaks about his mother with tenderness and protectiveness, and about his younger self with much less compassion. He still measures himself against an impossible standard, as though the frightened child in the hallway should have known how to stop a grown man. In session, he often minimizes what happened at first and then falls silent, jaw tight, when the weight of it catches up with him. The story of his life has become one of vigilance, competence, and quiet endurance, but beneath that is a boy who learned that home could turn dangerous without warning, and a young man who still lives as if he must be ready when it does.
